extracted.intended_audience: citizens and readers considering adoption of the U.S. Constitution; students and scholars of constitutional theory; general public
extracted.subtask_description: A series of political essays arguing for adoption of the proposed U.S. Constitution by setting out the advantages of union, the defects of the Confederation, and the necessary qualities of a national government to secure safety, liberty, and property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility of the Union
rubrics_metrics.description: The adoption of a national union promotes the political prosperity, safety, and welfare of the parts of the country and is preferable to dismemberment into separate confederacies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton proposes to discuss 'THE UTILITY OF THE UNION TO YOUR POLITICAL PROSPERITY' and to compare its advantages with the evils likely from dissolution; the essay urges examining advantages of union and the certain evils from its dissolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insufficiency of the Present Confederation
rubrics_metrics.description: The existing confederation is inadequate to preserve the Union and its defects make a stronger national government necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton states he will treat 'THE INSUFFICIENCY OF THE PRESENT CONFEDERATION TO PRESERVE THAT UNION' and answer objections to the proposed Constitution based on that insufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of an Energetic Government
rubrics_metrics.description: A government at least equally energetic with the one proposed is necessary to achieve preservation of the Union, security, and effective administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton lists 'THE NECESSITY OF A GOVERNMENT AT LEAST EQUALLY ENERGETIC WITH THE ONE PROPOSED, TO THE ATTAINMENT OF THIS OBJECT' as a primary point of discussion and contrasts vigor of government with security of liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conformity to Principles of Republican Government
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed Constitution should conform to the true principles of republican government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton plans to evaluate 'THE CONFORMITY OF THE PROPOSED CONSTITUTION TO THE TRUE PRINCIPLES OF REPUBLICAN GOVERNMENT' and defend it against objections that energy implies despotism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy to State Constitutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine the proposed Constitution's analogy to state constitutions to assess its reasonableness and republican character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton intends to compare the proposed national plan with existing state constitutions as part of his defense ('ITS ANALOGY TO YOUR OWN STATE CONSTITUTION').

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional Security for Republican Government, Liberty, and Property
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether adoption of the Constitution will afford additional security to the preservation of republican government, liberty, and property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton lists 'THE ADDITIONAL SECURITY WHICH ITS ADOPTION WILL AFFORD TO THE PRESERVATION OF THAT SPECIES OF GOVERNMENT, TO LIBERTY, AND TO PROPERTY' as a key evaluative dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to Cede Some Natural Rights to Government
rubrics_metrics.description: When instituting government, the people must cede some of their natural rights in order to vest it with requisite powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jay emphasizes the 'indispensable necessity of government' and that by instituting it people must give government certain powers — a criterion for judging the proper scope of governmental authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union vs. Division: Which Best Serves Public Interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether it is in the people's interest to be one nation under a federal government or to divide into separate confederacies with similar powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jay argues readers should weigh the consequences and practical effects of unity versus multiple confederacies, considering commerce, security, and common character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust in Deliberative Bodies' Judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Give weight to the judgment of deliberative bodies (e.g., the Philadelphia convention) composed of experienced, reputable men when considering constitutional plans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jay asks readers to consider the convention's composition of distinguished and experienced men and to respect their unanimous recommendation as informative evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Security from Foreign Force and Influence via Union
rubrics_metrics.description: A cordial union under an efficient national government affords the best security against hostilities from abroad and foreign influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jay's essays argue at length that unity reduces causes of war, makes diplomatic compliance uniform, and improves capacity to repel or deter foreign aggression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize Causes of War by Reducing Fragmentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of wars is proportionate to the number and weight of causes that provoke them; a united nation gives fewer just causes of war than a disunited set of states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that unified treaty observance, consistent judicial interpretation, and centralized responsibility reduce provocation and misunderstandings leading to war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform Interpretation and Execution of Treaties and International Law
rubrics_metrics.description: Treaties and laws of nations should be expounded and executed in one consistent sense by a national government rather than variably by multiple state courts and governments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jay stresses that national courts and a single administration will prevent contradictory adjudications and policy that could provoke foreign disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: National Government Attracts Better Officials
rubrics_metrics.description: A national government, with a wider field for choice, will generally attract and appoint the best-qualified persons to manage national affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of its scope and resources, the national government will staff administration and judiciary with wiser, more systematic personnel than many individual states can.

rubrics_metrics.name: National Government Less Susceptible to Local Temptations
rubrics_metrics.description: A central government is less likely to be swayed by local prospect of present loss or advantage that might induce violations of treaties or justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jay argues that temptations to swerve from justice are often local and that a national government not affected by state-specific circumstances can better preserve good faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevention and Punishment of State-Caused Hostilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The national government must have competency and inclination to prevent or punish aggressions provoked by individual states (e.g., Indian hostilities caused by state misconduct).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jay notes examples where state conduct provoked wars and argues a central authority would be better poised to prevent and address such provocations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding Invitation to Hostility: Economic and Naval Power
rubrics_metrics.description: A national policy should place the country in a situation that does not invite hostility — by managing commerce, navigation, and naval resources prudently to avoid provoking rivals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jay cautions that commercial rivalry (fisheries, navigation, China/India trade) can create jealousy; prudent national management reduces pretexts for war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unified Defense and Militia Organization
rubrics_metrics.description: A single government can more effectively organize, discipline, and deploy militia and naval/army resources than multiple independent governments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jay compares the hypothetical division of Britain's militia/fleet to illustrate inefficiency of divided commands and emphasizes consolidated command and resource application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diplomatic Credibility and Capacity of a United Nation
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong, united nation is more likely to obtain satisfactory acknowledgments, explanations, and compensations from foreign powers than an individual state or weak confederacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses historical examples (e.g., Genoa and Louis XIV) to show how national dignity and power affect diplomatic outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of Passionate and Misleading Political Advocacy
rubrics_metrics.description: When deliberating constitutional questions, be cautious of arguments driven by passions, prejudices, personal interest, or the loudness of declamation rather than evidence of truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton warns against inflammatory party spirit, ambition, and avarice masquerading as public virtue; he urges sober, candid consideration of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of Public Good Over Particular Interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate plans by their effects on the public good, not by how they advantage particular classes who might resist loss of state office, emolument, or power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton identifies particular interests (state officeholders, ambitious men) as obstacles and urges judgment unperplexed by private considerations.
